assignments.title: First-Contact Story Project
assignments.html:
First-Contact Story Project
Module Major Work
130 points600 to 900 words3 files
Write a story about a first contact. At its turning point, one character gives a speech. Then perform that speech from memory.
The module question: what do we lose when we assume we understand the other?
What you make
 
1
The story
600 to 900 words: a traveler, an unfamiliar place, a being unlike them, and a wrong idea that costs something
→
2
The speech
150 to 250 words, inside the story at the change, in a formal, unhurried voice like the Oyarsa’s
→
3
The recording
About one minute: the speech, performed from memory
Where you build it
 
1
Plan Your Story
First-Contact Story Project 1, in this module: brainstorm, then outline.
2
Write Your Story
First-Contact Story Project 2: draft each part, write and rehearse the speech, revise, and download your story as a Word file.
Turn in three files, in one submission
 
1
Project PDF
From the Turn In tab of Write Your Story. It holds both project lessons.
2
Your story
LastName_FirstName_OOTSPStory_ELA8.docx, saved in OneDrive → Optima → ELA → ELA8.
3
Your recording
The speech, audio or video: LastName_FirstName_OOTSPSpeech_ELA8
Your own characters and sentences. Nothing copied from Lewis.
How it is graded
 
Imitation of Lewis’s technique (sensory world-building)
ExcellentThe world is built impression by impression, through the senses in a believable order, so the reader discovers it as the traveler does.
ProficientThe world is built largely through the senses; most details arrive before they are explained.
DevelopingSome sensory detail appears, but the world is often told rather than shown.
BeginningThe world is mostly named or explained, with little sensory building.
Narrative craft (clear arc and point of view)
ExcellentA clear arc with a meaningful change; a steady, consistent point of view throughout.
ProficientA clear arc and a mostly consistent point of view.
DevelopingAn arc is present but uneven; point of view slips in places.
BeginningLittle sense of arc; point of view is unclear or shifts often.
Sensory and figurative language
ExcellentFresh, precise images and well-chosen comparisons that make the strange world vivid.
ProficientClear images and some effective figurative language.
DevelopingSome images, but often general or repeated; little figurative language.
BeginningVague or flat language; the world is hard to picture.
Clarity and correctness of prose
ExcellentClean, controlled sentences; varied structure; errors are rare and do not distract.
ProficientMostly clean sentences; minor errors that do not obscure meaning.
DevelopingSeveral run-ons, fragments, or splices that slow the reader.
BeginningFrequent errors that often make meaning unclear.
The speech: voice & style imitation
ExcellentSentence rhythm, word choice, and tone consistently sound like Lewis’s world: long, gathered sentences, restrained detail, wonder braided with moral seriousness.
ProficientThe voice mostly sounds like Lewis’s world, with occasional lines that slip into modern or casual phrasing.
DevelopingSome formal or old-fashioned phrasing appears, but much of the speech reads like ordinary modern speech.
BeginningThe speech does not attempt a formal voice; it reads as the student’s own ordinary speech with a name attached.
The speech: original content
ExcellentEvery line is the student’s own words; the speech is specific, believable for the character who gives it, and reveals something the story has not yet said.
ProficientThe content is original and fits the character; the moment is clear, if less surprising.
DevelopingThe content is original but generic; the character’s reasoning is vague.
BeginningThe speech borrows heavily from the novel’s actual lines rather than the student’s own words.
Delivery
ExcellentDelivered from memory with clear pacing, audible volume, and a voice and posture that fit the character; sounds like speech, not reading.
ProficientDelivered with only brief glances at notes; pacing and volume are mostly clear.
DevelopingDelivered mostly by reading; pacing is rushed or volume is hard to hear in places.
BeginningRead flatly with little preparation; difficult to follow as a spoken performance.
Done when
 
☐Story: 600 to 900 words, with a title; senses first, a clear arc, one point of view.
☐Assuming costs the traveler something.
☐Speech: 150 to 250 words, at the change, every sentence your own.
☐Recording: the speech from memory, easy to hear.
☐All three files uploaded together.

assignments.title: Independent Reading Check — Q2
assignments.html:
Q2 Independent Reading Check. This is the Q2 check on the book you chose for yourself this quarter.

📖 Your independent reading book

Every quarter you choose one book of your own and read it alongside our class texts. This is where you show what you read. It is not a book report and there is no essay.

Pick your book from the Optima Independent Reading menu. Two rules:

  • You may not choose a book our class is reading this year. Check the syllabus.
  • Want something that is not on the menu? Ask your teacher first.

🎬 Choose how you show it

Record one of the following. Either one earns full credit.

Option 1 — Oral Book Response (about 3 minutes)

Answer these five questions out loud, in order. You may keep notes in front of you, but do not read a script word for word.

  1. What is the book, and how far did you get?

    2. Title, author, and honestly where you ended up. Finishing is the goal, but an honest “I got to chapter nine” is worth more than a vague answer.

  2. Pick one character. What do they want, and what is standing in the way?

    3. Name the want in your own words. “They want to be left alone” is a real answer. “They want to be happy” is not specific enough.

  3. Describe a moment where that character makes a choice you would not have made. Why did they make it?

    4. This is the question that shows you understood the character rather than just the plot. You have to explain their reasoning, not yours.

  4. Read one sentence or short passage you marked, and say why that one.

    5. Any reason counts as long as it is yours: it surprised you, it was beautiful, it explained something, you disagreed with it.

  5. Who should read this book, and who should skip it?

    6. Be specific about the reader you have in mind.

Option 2 — Dramatic Reading (about 3 minutes)

  1. Choose a passage from your book, roughly 150 to 300 words, where a character is under pressure — deciding something, arguing, afraid, or hiding something.
  2. Read it aloud as that character. Decide before you record what this character wants in this moment, then let your pace, volume, and pauses show it.
  3. Then talk for about a minute: who is this character, what do they want here, and what did you do with your voice to show it? Name one specific choice you made.

The passage is your own copy of your own book, read by you. That is the point of the exercise.

✅ Success criteria

  • ☐ My book is from the menu (or teacher-approved) and is not a class text this year.
  • ☐ I recorded Option 1 or Option 2, all the way through.
  • ☐ I talked about a character, not only what happened.
  • ☐ I am looking at the camera and speaking clearly enough to be understood.
